subsystems.name: Pressurised modules
subsystems.role: shirtsleeve working space that protects equipment and crew from vacuum and temperature swings.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal control
subsystems.role: supplies tens of kilowatts for furnaces and keeps heat rejection working in vacuum.

subsystems.name: Microgravity process equipment
subsystems.role: the actual production plant: furnaces, fibre-drawing rigs, bioreactors, printers.

subsystems.name: Robotics and external assembly
subsystems.role: builds and handles structures too large or too delicate for people to move by hand.

subsystems.name: Logistics and downmass
subsystems.role: brings feedstock up and returns finished product to Earth.

subsystems.name: Control and quality assurance
subsystems.role: runs processes with little or no crew, and checks that the product is good.

buildSteps.title: Choose the orbit
buildSteps.detail: Low Earth orbit around 400 km is reachable and crew-serviced, but tenuous air drag causes tiny accelerations; higher orbits give cleaner microgravity at the cost of launch energy.

buildSteps.title: Launch modules and dock them
buildSteps.detail: Rigid pressure modules are launched on heavy-lift rockets and joined in orbit, either automatically or by a robotic arm.

buildSteps.title: Fit out the interior
buildSteps.detail: Standard equipment racks are installed with power, data, cooling and ventilation so that experiments can be swapped in and out.

buildSteps.title: Install process equipment
buildSteps.detail: Furnaces for glass and crystal growth, fibre-drawing rigs, bioreactors and printers are mounted on vibration-isolated racks.

buildSteps.title: Run production campaigns
buildSteps.detail: Feedstock launched from Earth is processed over days or weeks — drawing optical fibre or growing crystals slowly enough for gravity-driven convection and settling to stay out of the way.

buildSteps.title: Assemble large structures outside
buildSteps.detail: Robotic arms, or suited crew, join trusses, antennas and support frames in vacuum, where they would be too big to launch folded.

buildSteps.title: Return the product
buildSteps.detail: Finished material is packed into a reentry capsule, survives several g of deceleration and about 1,600 °C at the heat shield, then lands or splashes down for recovery.

buildSteps.title: Automate and scale
buildSteps.detail: Crew time and resupply flights dominate cost, so the hub has to evolve from tended experiments into unattended production lines.

prerequisites.why: flight costs have fallen sharply, but a manufacturing hub needs frequent, cheap and reliable upmass.
optical fibre, protein crystals and some alloys behave better without convection and settling, but yields and purity are still being characterised.
very little mass can be brought back from orbit today, and returning fragile products intact is hard.
robotic arms have operated outside stations for decades, but free-flying assembly of large structures is still early.
a profitable hub cannot depend on astronauts tending every batch.

prerequisites.tech: Products that beat Earth-made ones on price
prerequisites.why: without a clear commercial advantage, the cost of orbit cannot be justified.

pathway.milestone: experiments on crewed orbital stations producing optical fibre, crystals and biological tissue, with small capsules returning samples
pathway.unlocks: evidence about which products genuinely benefit from microgravity.

pathway.milestone: free-flying, commercially operated platforms in low Earth orbit
pathway.unlocks: more power, cleaner microgravity and no dependence on a single station.

pathway.milestone: uncrewed, automated production lines with routine return flights
pathway.unlocks: volumes high enough to test real markets.

pathway.milestone: orbital hubs that also assemble large structures and serve as depots
pathway.unlocks: a manufacturing and servicing economy in orbit rather than one-off experiments.
